# Volume 4 — CHAPTER 24 THE LIFE-BOOK OF CAPTAIN SAUL

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“A small brown cocoon of an idea is in my possession, one that might perhaps grow into a grand moth of realization,” Nell remarked to Hugh upon her arrival at the house. He had come back sooner than she anticipated, and was relishing a piece of Tabitha’s cherry pie. Tabitha was waiting nearby, resembling a somewhat severe yet kindly protective angel, deriving just as much joy from seeing Hugh consume the pie as he experienced while consuming it.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0000 }

“What are you thinking?” he inquired.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0001 }

“I won’t inform you right now—not until I determine whether I can accomplish this.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0002 }

“What kind of a fellow is Treleaven?”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0003 }

“Oh, extremely pleasant, and rather handsome.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0004 }

“Such exquisite ears, doctor, dear,” Tabitha chimed in with great pleasure.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0005 }

“By my estimate, his age is roughly thirty or thirty-five, and he intends to draft a book. A pleasant voice is paired with his charming smile, and he possesses a good sense of style. In some way, he appears as though his journey through life has not been completely simple.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0006 }

When the next evening arrived, Adrian Treleaven brought a message from Lorna to Nell; after spending the hours of sunset in the garden, they took the small vessel Hugh had prepared for summer trips out on the harbor for a sail under the moon. Their liking for Adrian was immense, and they experienced that sense of long acquaintance that marks the kinship of the house of Joseph. “He is as nice as his ears, Mrs. Doctor, dear,” Tabitha remarked after his departure. He had informed Tabitha that her strawberry shortcake surpassed anything he had previously eaten, winning over Tabitha’s impressionable heart for eternity.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0007 }

“There is a way about him,” she mused while tidying away the remains of the meal. “That he remains unmarried is truly strange, because a person of his sort could win anyone just by asking. Well, perhaps he resembles me and has hitherto failed to encounter his proper match.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0008 }

As she cleaned the dishes from the evening meal, Tabitha truly became rather imaginative in her thoughts.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0009 }

When two nights had passed, Nell brought Adrian Treleaven along to Seven Gulls Point so he could be introduced to Captain Saul. The western wind was turning the clover fields pale beside the harbor shore, while Captain Saul had put one of his most splendid sunsets on display. He had only recently come back from a voyage across the harbor.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0010 }

“It fell to me to visit Henry Pollack and inform him that his end was near. No one else possessed the courage to break the news. A terrible reaction was anticipated from him, given his desperate determination to survive and his extensive preparations for the autumn. It was his wife's belief that he should be informed and that I was the most suitable person to impart the truth about his fatal condition. Henry and I share a long friendship—we crewed the Gray Gull together over many years. So, I traveled there and took a chair beside Henry’s mattress, and I spoke to him, saying I, directly and without fuss, because when news must be shared it is best delivered immediately, saying I, 'Mate, I reckon you’ve got your sailing orders this time,’ I was trembling somewhat internally, since delivering news of impending death to someone completely unaware of it is a fearful duty. Yet to my amazement, Mistress Carrow, Henry gazes at me, his shriveled face featuring those luminous, ancient dark eyes, and he speaks, saying he, 'Tell me something I don’t know, Saul Garrick, if you want to give me information. I’ve known THAT for a week.’ Speechless from shock, I watched as Henry gave a quiet laugh. 'To see you coming in here,’ saying he, 'with your face as solemn as a tombstone and sitting down there with your hands clasped over your stomach, and passing me out a blue-mouldy old item of news like that! It’d make a cat laugh, Saul Garrick,’ saying he. 'Who told you?’ saying I, foolishly. 'Nobody,’ saying he. 'A week ago Tuesday night I was lying here awake—and I jest knew. I’d suspicioned it before, but then I KNEW. I’ve been keeping up for the wife’s sake. And I’d LIKE to have got that barn built, for Eben’ll never get it right. But anyhow, now that you’ve eased your mind, Saul, put on a smile and tell me something interesting,’ Indeed, that was the situation. Everyone had been terrified of informing him, yet he was aware the whole duration. It is remarkable how nature cares for us, isn't it, and reveals what we ought to understand when the moment arrives? Have I ever related the story to you concerning the time Henry caught a fish hook in his nose, Mistress Carrow?”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0011 }

“No.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0012 }

“Well, he and I shared a laugh about it today. Almost thirty years ago, it took place. A group of us, including him and me, went out mackerel fishing one day. The day was wonderful—a school of mackerel that large was something I had never seen in the gulf—and as everyone grew excited, Henry became very reckless and managed to plunge a fish hook straight through a side of his nose. Well, that was his situation; a barb was on one end and a large lead piece was on the other, meaning pulling it out was impossible. Taking him to shore right away was our wish, but Henry showed pluck; he declared he’d be jiggered if he’d abandon such a school for anything less than lockjaw; after that he continued fishing, pulling them in rapidly while groaning in between. Eventually the school moved on and we returned with a full catch; acquiring a file, I started trying to file through the hook. My intention was to be as gentle as possible, but hearing Henry was an experience you should have had—actually, you shouldn't have either. It was fortunate that no ladies were present. Swearing was not Henry's habit, but over time he had heard a few such expressions along the coast, and retrieving them all from his memory, he launched them at me. Ultimately he announced that he was unable to bear it and that I lacked any feelings of sympathy. Therefore we harnessed the horse and I took him in a wagon to a physician in Port Marlow, a distance of thirty-five miles—in those times there were none closer—while that confounded hook remained dangling from his nose. Upon our arrival, old Dr. Crabb simply picked up a file and filed the hook in the exact same manner I had attempted, except he did not care in the least about being gentle!”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0013 }

Seeing his longtime companion once again had brought back numerous memories for Captain Saul, who was currently immersed in a flood of past experiences.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0014 }

“Today, Henry was inquiring whether I recalled when Alexander MacAllister’s boat was blessed by old Father Chiniquy. It is another strange story—and completely true. I was aboard the boat myself. One morning at dawn, him and I went out in the boat belonging to Alexander MacAllister. Additionally, a French boy was in the boat—naturally a Catholic. As you are aware, old Father Chiniquy had become a Protestant, meaning the Catholics did not care for him much. Anyway, we remained out in the gulf under the scorching sun until midday, without getting a single bite. When we landed, old Father Chiniquy needed to depart, so in his courteous manner he stated, 'I’m very sorry I cannot go out with you dis afternoon, Mr. MacAllister, but I leave you my blessing. You will catch a t’ousand dis afternoon. 'Well, our catch was not a thousand, yet we retrieved precisely nine hundred and ninety-nine—the largest haul for a little boat across the entire north shore during that summer. Strange, wasn't it? Alexander MacAllister asked Andrew Peters, 'Well, and what do you think of Father Chiniquy now?’ 'Vell,’ Andrew grumbled, 'I t’ink de old devil has got a blessing left yet.’ Goodness, how Henry laughed about that today!”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0015 }

“Have you any idea who Mr. Treleaven is, Captain Saul?” Nell inquired, observing that Captain Saul’s stream of memories had temporarily dried up. “I would like you to make a guess.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0016 }

A shake of his head came from Captain Saul.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0017 }

“I was never skilled at making guesses, Mistress Carrow, but even so, upon entering I reflected, ‘Where did I previously encounter those eyes?’—because I TRULY have encountered them.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0018 }

“Recall a September morning from a long time in the past,” Nell said quietly. “Picture a vessel coming into the harbor—a vessel anticipated for a long period and given up on. Picture the day when the Royal William arrived and the initial glimpse you caught of the schoolmaster’s bride.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0019 }

Captain Saul leaped to his feet.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0020 }

“Those are Damaris Tremayne’s eyes,” he nearly yelled. “You cannot be her son—it must be that you are her—”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0021 }

“Grandson; indeed, my mother was Alice Tremayne.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0022 }

Captain Saul plunged downward toward Adrian Treleaven and gripped his hand once more.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0023 }

“The child of Alice Tremayne! My goodness, you are truly welcome! On numerous occasions I have pondered where the schoolmaster’s progeny resided. I was aware that not one remained on the Island. Alice—Alice—the initial infant who came into the world inside that tiny dwelling. Never did a newborn deliver such happiness! A hundred times I bounced her on my knee. It was off my lap that she managed her very first solitary steps. Clearly I recall her mother's countenance gazing at her—and almost sixty years have passed since then. Does she still draw breath?”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0024 }

“No, my mother passed away while I was still just a young boy.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0025 }

“Oh, it feels wrong for me to still be alive to learn of that,” Captain Saul sighed. “However, seeing you fills my heart with joy. For a brief moment, it has restored my youth. You have not yet learned how great a blessing THAT is. Mistress Carrow present possesses the ability—she accomplishes it for me fairly frequently.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0026 }

When he found out that Adrian Treleaven was a person he referred to as a “real writing man,” Captain Saul became even more thrilled. He looked upon him as though he were a higher order of person. Captain Saul was aware of Nell’s writing, yet he had never given much weight to the matter. It was Captain Saul’s view that women were charming beings who should be granted the right to vote along with whatever else they desired, bless their hearts; nevertheless, he lacked faith in their ability to write.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0027 }

“Jest take a look at A Mad Love,” he was prone to object. “That was written by a woman and jest look at the result—it has one hundred and three chapters even though ten would have sufficed to tell everything. Knowing when to stop is something a writing woman never manages; there lies the issue. Knowing when to stop is the p’int of good writing.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0028 }

“Captain Saul, Mr. Treleaven wishes to listen to a few of your tales,” Nell remarked. “Relate to him the story concerning the captain who lost his mind and believed he was the Flying Dutchman.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0029 }

Captain Saul’s finest tale was this one. Horror and humor were blended within it, and even though Nell had listened to it a number of times, she chuckled just as warmly and shuddered just as terrifyingly over it as Mr. Treleaven did. Subsequent stories came next, because Captain Saul possessed a group of listeners completely to his liking. He recounted how a steamer had collided with his vessel; how Malay pirates had boarded him; how his vessel had caught fire; how he aided a political prisoner in escaping from a South African republic; how he had been shipwrecked one autumn on the Magdalens and remained stuck there for the winter; how a tiger had escaped on shipboard; how his crew had mutinied and left him marooned on a desolate island—Captain Saul narrated these and numerous other stories, whether tragic, humorous, or bizarre. His audience felt and comprehended all of them—the sea’s mystery, the charm of distant territories, the attraction of adventure, and the world’s laughter. Resting his head on his hand while the First Mate purred upon his knee, Adrian Treleaven listened, his shining eyes fixed on Captain Saul’s rough, expressive face.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0030 }

“Will you not allow Mr. Treleaven to inspect your life-book, Captain Saul?” Nell inquired, after Captain Saul ultimately announced that the telling of tales had to cease for the moment.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0031 }

“Oh, THAT isn't something he wants to be bothered by,” Captain Saul objected, though he was secretly longing to display it.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0032 }

“Captain Garrick, nothing would please me more than viewing it,” Adrian stated. “It will be well worth the sight if it possesses even half the wonder of your stories.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0033 }

Captain Saul, feigning unwillingness, pulled his life-book from his ancient chest and passed it over to Adrian.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0034 }

“It is my guess that you will not want to struggle for very long with my old handwriting. My education was quite limited,” he remarked in a casual tone. “I merely penned that piece to entertain my nephew Joe. He has a constant desire for tales. He arrives here yesterday and tells me, in a somewhat reproachful manner, while I was hoisting a codfish weighing twenty pounds out of my vessel, 'Uncle Saul, ain’t a codfish a dumb animal?’ You see, I had been explaining to him that he ought to be truly gentle with dumb animals, and never cause them any harm. I escaped the difficult situation by claiming that a codfish was sufficiently dumb but was not an animal, yet Joe failed to appear convinced, and I lacked satisfaction myself. A person must exercise extreme caution regarding what they impart to those little youngsters. THEY are capable of seeing right through you.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0035 }

As he spoke, Captain Saul kept a side-glance on Adrian Treleaven, who was scrutinizing the life-book; and when he noticed soon after that his visitor was engrossed in what he was reading, he faced his cupboard with a smile and set about brewing tea. Adrian Treleaven parted from the life-book—showing the same unwillingness that a miser displays when forced away from his fortune—only as long as it took to consume his tea, after which he eagerly went back to reading.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0036 }

“Oh, you can bring that item back to your house if you wish,” remarked Captain Saul, pretending that the “thing” was not the item he held most dear. “I am required to head below and draw my vessel a little higher along the skids. A gust is approaching. Were you paying attention to the heavens this evening?
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0037 }

“When mares’ tails and mackerel skies appear, grand vessels must reduce the canvas they wear.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0038 }

The proposal regarding the life-book was accepted with pleasure by Adrian Treleaven. As they were returning home, the tale of lost Margaret was recounted to him by Nell.
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0039 }

“That aged captain is a marvelous old man,” he remarked. “What an existence he has had! Indeed, that person experienced a greater number of adventures during a single week of his existence than the majority of us experience over a whole life. Do you truly believe that his stories are entirely genuine?”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0040 }

“Indeed I do. Captain Saul is undoubtedly incapable of lying; furthermore, the local inhabitants all confirm that events occurred precisely as he describes. Numerous former crew members of his were once living to verify his story. He remains a rare survivor of the traditional St. Brendan’s Island sea-captains, a group that has nearly vanished.”
{: #nw-v04-c24-p0041 }
